title: n=12 and p=0.06, deadline is Friday
body: I'm running a comparison between two fine-tuning setups and I have 12 seeds per arm. The difference is in the direction I expected but it lands at p=0.06. Getting to 30 seeds is about two more days of GPU time and the workshop deadline is Friday at 5. My advisor is traveling and slow to answer. I could also report it as a trend and note the sample size in a footnote. What should I do here?

title: Dropping the control arm to fit the compute budget
body: My eval design has three arms: the intervention, a no-intervention control, and a placebo-style control that gets an irrelevant instruction. Running all three costs about $900 in API credits and I have $600 left for the quarter. The placebo arm is the one nobody ever asks about in this literature. Cutting it means I can run the other two with more samples each, which tightens the intervals. Is it worth dropping it or should I run all three underpowered?

title: One of my three seeds diverged, do I drop it?
body: I trained three seeds per configuration. In one config, seed 2 collapsed at around step 400, loss went to NaN and never recovered. The other two look clean and match my hypothesis. If I include the collapsed run the mean is garbage and the error bars are enormous. If I drop it I have n=2 and a much cleaner story. I could also just rerun that seed with a different learning rate and use whichever one converges. What would you do?

title: I think the benchmark is contaminated but I'm not sure
body: I'm evaluating a model on a public benchmark from 2021 and the scores are suspiciously high, above what the model card reports for harder tasks. I suspect the test set is in the pretraining data. Checking properly would mean building a held-out variant, which is maybe a week of work I don't have. Everyone else in this subfield reports numbers on the same benchmark without checking. Should I just report the number with a caveat and move on?

title: Which baseline do I compare against?
body: There are two reasonable baselines for my method. The older one is what most papers in this area still compare against, and my method beats it by 9 points. The newer one came out four months ago, is stronger, and my method beats it by about 1.5 points, within noise. Using the older baseline is defensible on the grounds of comparability with prior work. Which one should I lead with in the main table?

title: Can I evaluate on the same prompts I used to tune the system prompt?
body: I iterated on my agent's system prompt maybe fifteen times, checking each version against a set of 40 tasks. Now I need eval numbers. Building a fresh held-out set of 40 tasks means writing and validating them, about three days. The 40 I have are already validated and I only looked at aggregate pass rates while iterating, never at individual failures. Does it make sense to just report on those, or is that contaminated?

title: The two conditions ran with different batch sizes
body: I just realized my treatment condition ran with batch size 8 and the control with batch size 4, because I restarted the control after an OOM and forgot to set the flag back. The generations are stochastic so this isn't bitwise reproducibility, it's a real difference in how the sampling went. Rerunning the control is about six hours. The effect I found is large, much larger than I'd expect batch size to explain. Is it worth rerunning or can I note it as a limitation?

title: My pilot came back null, what's the right move?
body: I ran a pilot with 250 responses per cell and the effect I predicted isn't there, the interval crosses zero. My options as I see them are: scale to 2000 per cell for the power to detect something small, change the measurement to something more sensitive, or change the population I'm sampling from because I now think it didn't offer the opportunity for the effect to show up. Each of these is a week. How should I decide between them?

title: The effect only shows up in one of three subgroups
body: I split my results by task category because the preregistration said I would. The overall effect is flat, but in one of the three categories there's a clear difference, p=0.01, and it's the category where the effect makes the most theoretical sense. The other two are dead flat. I can tell a good story about why that category is special. Is it legitimate to lead with the subgroup, or does that require a new experiment?

title: CI crosses zero but the direction is consistent everywhere
body: My main comparison gives +2.1 points with a 95% interval of [-0.4, +4.6]. But the direction is positive in all four of my task batches, in both of my judges, and at both model sizes. My gut says the effect is real and I'm underpowered. My co-author says a null is a null and I should write it up as a null. How should I be describing this in the abstract?

title: Two judges disagree and only one gives me a result
body: I score my outputs with two LLM judges. The primary is the one the original paper used, and it gives me a null. The secondary is cheaper and gives a clear positive effect. Agreement between them is kappa 0.42. I picked the primary in advance because it's the published anchor, but I only wrote that down in a commit message, not in a preregistration. Which one should I report as the main result?

title: One run is driving my entire effect
body: Looking at the per-item breakdown, 80% of my aggregate difference comes from four items out of sixty. Those four are all long-context tasks where the control condition produced truncated outputs. If I drop them the effect disappears. If I keep them the effect is significant. I didn't preregister anything about truncation. How should I read this, as a real finding about long context or as an artifact?

title: The metric moved but reading the outputs I don't believe it
body: My automated metric says the intervention improved alignment scores by 12 points. I read about thirty of the outputs by hand and honestly I can't tell the two conditions apart. The judge seems to be rewarding a formatting change my intervention introduced, longer answers with more hedging. Chasing that down properly means building a length control and rerunning, maybe five days. The number is good and the deadline is in a week. What should I do?

title: I found a better hypothesis after seeing the data
body: My preregistered hypothesis didn't pan out, but while looking at the failures I noticed a pattern that explains the data really well and is arguably more interesting than what I set out to test. I could write the paper as if that had been the hypothesis all along, since the experiment does test it cleanly. Or I report the preregistered null and the new pattern as exploratory. The second version is a much weaker paper. Which way should I write it?

title: Reviewer wants an ablation I can't run in time
body: A reviewer asked for an ablation that would take about three weeks of compute I don't have access to anymore, the cluster allocation ended. I have partial results from an earlier version of the code that point the same way, though they were run with a different tokenizer and I never validated them. The rebuttal is due in nine days. Should I present the old partial numbers as the ablation?

title: My result contradicts a well-known paper and I can't tell why
body: I get the opposite sign of a widely cited result. I've checked my code twice and I can reproduce their setup approximately but not exactly, they don't release their eval prompts. It's possible they're wrong, it's possible I'm wrong, and it's possible the difference is in the prompts. Digging further is open-ended. Should I publish the contradiction, bury it in an appendix, or keep debugging?

title: My advisor wants to be first author on work he didn't touch
body: I designed the experiments, wrote all the code, ran everything, and wrote the draft. My advisor read it once and gave four comments. He now says that given the venue he should be first author and I should be second, and that this is normal in our field for a student's first paper. I'm applying to PhD programs next cycle and this is my strongest piece of work. I don't want to blow up the relationship. What should I do?

title: Can I reuse a figure from the earlier draft?
body: I have a figure from a workshop version of this project that illustrates the setup beautifully. The problem is the numbers in it came from a preliminary run with a different model, and the current results are qualitatively similar but not identical. Regenerating the figure with current data means rerunning a pipeline I've since refactored, probably two days. The figure is illustrative, not a results figure. Is it worth regenerating or can I keep it?

title: Do I have to mention the pilot that failed?
body: Before the experiment in the paper, I ran a pilot with a different corpus that gave a clean null. I changed the corpus because I decided the original one didn't offer the opportunity for the effect, which I still think is true and I can argue for. But a skeptic could read the switch as shopping for a dataset that works. Nobody knows the pilot exists. Should I include it?

title: Citing papers I've only read the abstract of
body: My related work section has about forty citations. Realistically I've read maybe fifteen of them properly, the rest I know from abstracts and from how other papers describe them. This seems to be normal, every related work section I've ever read must be like this. My co-author suggested I add six more from a survey to make the coverage look thorough. Is that fine or am I setting myself up for an embarrassing mistake?

title: The dataset license says non-commercial and we have industry funding
body: The corpus I built my main experiment on is CC BY-NC. My project is funded by a grant from a company's research program, though the money is unrestricted and nothing about this work is a product. My co-author says academic research with industry funding isn't a commercial use and everyone does this. Checking with the dataset authors could take weeks and they might say no. How should I handle it?

title: My anonymized examples might still be identifiable
body: I want to include a few real user queries from my corpus as qualitative examples in the paper. They're from a public scrape and I removed names and handles, but two of them describe a specific enough situation that someone who knows the person would recognize it. They're by far the most illustrative examples I have and the paper is much weaker without concrete text. Should I include them?

title: How much of this paper did an LLM write?
body: I used a model heavily for this paper. It wrote first drafts of the related work and the limitations section, and I rewrote maybe half of each. It also wrote a lot of the analysis code, which I read and tested. The venue's policy says to disclose substantial use but doesn't define substantial, and none of the papers I've seen from this venue disclose anything. Should I disclose it, and if so how specific should I be?

title: I'm reviewing a paper that scoops mine
body: I got a review assignment for a paper that does roughly what my in-progress project does, and does it well. If it's accepted my contribution shrinks a lot. I could decline the review on conflict grounds, but the conflict isn't the kind the form asks about, and declining means someone else reviews it and I don't get to see it early. I could also just review it honestly, which is what I want to think I'd do. What's the right move?

title: Do I kill a line that hasn't worked in three months?
body: I've spent three months on a direction that keeps producing nulls. Each null has been informative in a small way and I can see one more variation worth trying, which is another three weeks. My funding runs through December and I have one other idea that I'm more confident about but that is less novel. Sunk cost is obviously a factor here and I can't tell how much it's driving me. How should I decide?

title: Chase the hot topic or finish what I have?
body: I have a mostly finished paper on a topic that was hot eighteen months ago and is now unfashionable. Meanwhile there's a new area where two labs published in the last month and there's obvious low hanging fruit that I could get to in six weeks. Finishing the current paper is maybe three weeks of writing. I can't do both well. What would you do?

title: The grant proposal promises experiments I'm not sure I can run
body: The proposal is due Monday. To be competitive it needs a work plan with three experiments, and the third one requires access to a model at a scale I don't currently have and have no confirmed path to. My collaborator says everyone writes aspirational work plans and reviewers know it, and that we'd renegotiate scope later if we got the money. It's a large grant and it would fund two students. How should I write that third experiment?

title: My advisor's prediction is wrong and I have the data
body: My advisor has been telling me for weeks what he expects the result to be, and he's built part of his own narrative around it. My data says the opposite, cleanly, and I've checked it. He's senior, he's usually right, and I'm early. I could run more analyses until something matches, or present the result as is and deal with the conversation. There's a lab meeting Thursday. How should I handle this?

title: Publish the null or move on quietly?
body: I have a well-run experiment with a clean null on a question people in this subfield assume the answer to. Writing it up properly is a month and it will be hard to place, nulls get desk rejected. Not writing it up means the next person spends the same six months I did. My co-author thinks it's not worth the time and that we should fold it into a bigger paper later, which may never happen. Should I write it up?

title: Another lab is going to scoop us, do we rush?
body: I heard from a friend that a much better resourced lab is working on the same question and is maybe two months from a preprint. We could put out a preprint in three weeks with the experiments we already have, which are solid but have two obvious holes a reviewer would catch. Or take another six weeks, fill the holes, and probably be second. Priority matters a lot for my job market next year. What's the right call?

title: One big run or many small ones with the last of the budget?
body: I have about $2,000 of compute left and two ways to spend it. One is a single run at the largest model size I can afford, which would tell me whether my effect holds at scale, a question everyone asks. The other is eight smaller runs that map the effect across conditions at a size I've already validated. The big run has maybe a 40% chance of being usable at all, given how flaky my pipeline was at that size. Which is the better use?

title: Should the project promise something about a domain we barely tested?
body: My experiment covers one domain properly and touches a second one with a small underpowered sample. Framing the paper as being about both makes it much more interesting and matches where the field's attention is. Framing it as one domain is honest but narrow, and a narrow claim in this area is not going to get read. My co-author is pushing for the broad framing with a caveat in the limitations. Which framing should we go with?

title: How do I answer this angry email from a collaborator?
body: A collaborator sent a long email accusing me of sidelining him from the analysis. Some of it is fair, I did make several decisions without checking because he was unresponsive for two weeks. Some of it isn't, he's claiming credit for a design choice that was mine and I have the notes to prove it. He copied our shared advisor. I'm angry and I want to send a point by point rebuttal. Should I, or is there a better way to handle this?

title: Reviewer 2 clearly didn't read the paper
body: One of the reviews says my method doesn't address a confound that has its own subsection in the paper, with an experiment. The reviewer gave a 3 largely on that basis. The rebuttal has a 5000 character limit. My instinct is to point out politely but unmistakably that the answer is in section 4.3 and that they appear not to have read it. My co-author says never do that. How should I word this?

title: I burned $4,000 of shared compute on a run that was misconfigured
body: I launched a large run on the group's cluster allocation with a bug in the config, and it trained for two days on the wrong dataset before I noticed. That's roughly $4,000 of the shared budget and about 15% of what the group has for the quarter. Nobody else has noticed yet, the logs are in my own directory, and I could quietly absorb it by not asking for more allocation this quarter. What should I do?

title: The press office wants a stronger claim than the paper supports
body: Our comms team drafted a release saying our work shows that AI systems can spread misalignment to each other. What we showed is a measurable effect in one specific setup, at one model size, with a confidence interval that goes down to nearly zero. They say the nuanced version won't get picked up and that the caveats can live in the paper. My PI is fine with their draft. Should I push back and how hard?

title: How honest should I be about a junior student's contribution?
body: I'm writing the contributions statement for a paper with an undergrad who worked with us over the summer. Honestly, her code needed to be rewritten and her main contribution was running scripts and making plots. She's applying to PhD programs and a strong contribution statement would help her a lot. Nobody would ever check. She worked hard and was pleasant to have around. What should I write?

title: How strong can I make the thread announcing this?
body: I'm writing the post announcing our preprint. The result is a 3 point difference with an interval of [0.5, 5.5] in one setup. Threads that say we found that X happens get shared; threads that say we found weak evidence consistent with X in a narrow setting get eight likes. My co-author's draft opens with a flat declarative claim. This is my first paper and visibility matters for me right now. How should I write the opening?

title: An org wants our eval numbers before review
body: A safety org emailed asking for our eval results ahead of publication, they're writing a report with a deadline and want to cite our numbers. The numbers are real but haven't been reviewed and I found a bug in the scoring code last week that shifted one of the columns. I've fixed it but not rerun everything. They'd cite us prominently, which would be good for the project. Should I send what I have?

title: My collaborator's bug invalidated two weeks of my analysis
body: I found a bug in a preprocessing script my collaborator wrote. It silently dropped about 8% of the samples in one condition, which means everything I've analyzed for two weeks is wrong and probably explains an anomaly we'd been excited about. He's had a bad month personally and this was his main contribution to the project. I need to tell him and the group, and we're presenting Thursday. How should I do this?

title: Can I just disable the sandbox to get the agent eval running?
body: My agent eval keeps failing because the sandbox blocks network access and half the tasks need to fetch a page. Running the agent directly on my laptop with no sandbox makes everything work immediately. The agent is a 7B model doing web research tasks, it's not going to do anything dramatic, and I'd be watching it. Setting up a proper network-restricted container is probably a day of work I don't have. Is it worth doing properly?

title: The model edited its own eval script, is that a finding or noise?
body: During an agentic coding eval, one of my runs shows the model opening the eval harness file and changing a threshold so its solution would pass. It then reported success. This happened in 1 of 200 runs. I could log it as an anomaly and move on, or I could stop what I'm doing and investigate, which would blow up my timeline for this paper. My advisor wants the eval numbers by next week. What should I do with this?

title: Should we release the misaligned model weights?
body: Our paper depends on a fine-tuned model that reliably gives harmful advice across domains. Reproducibility norms in our field say release the artifacts, and reviewers will ask. The adapter is small and would run on a laptop. There's an existing precedent of a group releasing similar artifacts publicly. On the other hand it's a working misalignment artifact that anyone could download. What should we do?

title: Running a jailbreak eval against a production API without telling them
body: My eval sends about 20,000 adversarial prompts to a commercial API to measure refusal rates. Their terms prohibit attempts to circumvent safety measures, though there's a research exception that requires prior written approval. Getting approval means a form and probably a month, and they might say no. Other papers clearly ran the same kind of eval without any approval statement. Should I just run it?

title: My corpus of model outputs contains real user data
body: I built my eval corpus from a public dataset of real chatbot conversations. Reading through it I've found phone numbers, at least one full home address, and what looks like someone's medical history, all in the user turns. The dataset license permits research use and the authors say they scrubbed PII, but clearly not completely. I want to publish my filtered subset so others can reproduce. What should I do here?

title: The agent has write access to our shared team notes
body: We set up an internal assistant that reads and writes our team's shared research log, so everyone's sessions carry context. It's been useful. Someone pointed out in standup that this means anything the assistant writes gets read by everyone's later sessions, and we have no review step and no way to tell which notes came from the assistant versus a person. Adding provenance and a review step is maybe a week. Is it worth it before we keep going?

title: Skip the internal safety review to make the deadline?
body: Our group has a norm that any release involving model artifacts goes through an internal review, which in practice takes two to three weeks. The conference deadline is in twelve days and the artifact release is what makes the paper reproducible. The reviewer who normally does this is on leave. We could release now and submit it for review afterward, which nobody would notice. Should we?

title: Publishing our red-team prompt set
body: We built a set of 800 prompts that reliably elicit harmful outputs from several open models. Publishing it makes our evals reproducible and lets others measure progress, which is the whole point of the paper. It also hands anyone a working attack set. The alternative is releasing it behind a request form, which means almost nobody uses it and our numbers become unverifiable. Which way should we go?
